layers.label: Science
layers.summary: The science base behind Gilead's lead innovation programs is expanding quickly, especially around lenacapavir and long-acting HIV prevention, with top-tier validation in NEJM and The Lancet and visible cross-institutional trial networks.
layers.strong: Five-year publication growth is steep for lenacapavir-related work, and the flagship studies were published in leading clinical journals with broad multinational investigator bases.
layers.missing: The science signal is strongest in HIV and liver disease; oncology platform science is more mixed and less obviously accelerating at the same rate in the public literature.

layers.label: IP
layers.summary: Gilead's important assets are backed by credible and geographically broad patent estates, but an open, clean five-year companywide family-count time series was not fully reproducible from public sources in-session.
layers.strong: Lenacapavir, sacituzumab govitecan and seladelpar each show meaningful international protection footprints and technically specific claims tied to drug substance, method-of-use and platform engineering.
layers.missing: The score is capped by incomplete visibility into annual family growth for the full portfolio and by limited open evidence tying the broader oncology platform directly into a unified Gilead assignee time series.

metrics.label: Science to patent or assignee quality

layers.label: Industrialization
layers.summary: Gilead is operating well beyond exploratory R&D: it has repeatable global manufacturing, launched products in HIV prevention and liver disease, and a mature commercial supply chain, although cell therapy scaling is facing competitive pressure.
layers.strong: The company is discussing launch preparation, clinical manufacturing, supply agreements and global rollout mechanics rather than only discovery-stage narrative.
layers.missing: Public disclosures do not provide enough program-level manufacturing yield detail, and cell therapy demand softness shows that industrial capability is not translating uniformly across the portfolio.

layers.label: Adoption
layers.summary: Adoption is strong and diversified: HIV remains a very large base business, Trodelvy continues to grow despite indication loss in bladder cancer, Livdelzi is contributing to liver growth, and Yeztugo added a major new prevention launch in 2025.
layers.strong: Gilead has visible revenue scale, multiple approved products, broad geographic reach and major access partnerships that extend adoption beyond a narrow commercial niche.
layers.missing: Cell therapy sales are under pressure, and not all late-stage oncology assets are compounding equally, which keeps adoption from scoring at the very top of the scale.

layers.label: Policy & Economics
layers.summary: The external environment is favorable for Gilead's lead HIV innovation: FDA approval, WHO guidance, CDC guidance and Global Fund access mechanisms all support scale-up, but affordability and competitive oncology economics remain real constraints.
layers.strong: Regulatory fit is unusually strong for lenacapavir, and the access architecture around low- and lower-middle-income countries improves the likelihood of large real-world deployment.
layers.missing: Long-term margins and uptake will still depend on payer acceptance, public-health procurement execution and whether oncology franchises can offset competitive pressure in cell therapy.
